title: Channel Capacity
description: Describe noisy channels by transition matrices and find how many bits per use they can carry reliably.

study.title: Discrete memoryless channels
study.body: A **discrete memoryless channel** (DMC) takes an input symbol $x$ and produces an output symbol $y$ with probability $p(y|x)$, independently for every use. Collect these in a **transition matrix**: one row per input, one column per output, every row summing to 1. The binary symmetric channel (BSC) flips a bit with probability $p$:

study.title: Channel capacity
study.body: The mutual information $I(X;Y)$ depends on the channel and on how often the transmitter uses each input. The **capacity** is the largest value over all input distributions, in bits per channel use. A noiseless channel with $M$ inputs has $C = \log_2 M$; for symmetric channels a uniform input is optimal. Multiply by the number of channel uses per second for bit/s.

study.title: Explore: BSC and BEC
study.body: For the BSC a uniform input gives $H(Y)$ = 1 and $H(Y|X) = H(p)$, so $C = 1 - H(p)$. It is 1 bit at $p$ = 0 **and** at $p$ = 1 (just invert every bit) and 0 at $p$ = 0.5. The **binary erasure channel** (BEC) instead loses a bit with probability $\varepsilon$ and tells the receiver so: $C = 1 - \varepsilon$. Drag $p$: an erasure costs much less than an undetected error.

study.title: The binary erasure channel
study.body: Output 'e' marks an erased bit. With a uniform input, $H(X)$ = 1 and an erased bit leaves 1 bit of uncertainty, so $H(X|Y) = \varepsilon$ and $I = 1 - \varepsilon$. Erasures model packet losses detected by a checksum, or symbols the demodulator flags as unreliable. Feedback (retransmission) would also deliver exactly $1 - \varepsilon$ bits per use on average.

study.title: Symmetric channels
study.body: If every row of the transition matrix is a permutation of every other row and all column sums are equal, the channel is **symmetric** (Cover & Thomas call this weakly symmetric): a uniform input makes the output uniform and $C = \log_2|\mathcal Y| - H(\text{row})$. Example: a ternary channel that keeps a symbol with probability 0.8 and turns it into each other symbol with probability 0.1 has $C = \log_2 3 - H(0.8, 0.1, 0.1)$ = 1.585 − 0.922 = 0.663 bit per use.

study.title: The channel coding theorem
study.body: Send $k$ message bits as a codeword of $n$ channel symbols: the **rate** is $R = k/n$ bits per channel use. Shannon proved that for every $R < C$ there are codes whose error probability goes to zero as $n$ grows, and that for $R > C$ the error probability cannot be made small. Capacity is therefore a hard speed limit for reliable communication. The proof uses random codes; units 7 and 8 show practical codes.

study.title: Cascaded channels
study.body: Two BSCs in series form a BSC whose crossover probability is the chance that exactly one of them flips the bit. $n$ identical hops give $p_n = \tfrac12[1 - (1-2p)^n]$, which creeps towards 0.5: capacity can only drop along a chain (data-processing inequality), unless the relays decode and re-encode. For erasure channels the survival probabilities multiply.

steps.title: A channel is a table of probabilities
steps.body: A discrete memoryless channel turns input $x$ into output $y$ with probability $p(y|x)$, independently every time it is used. Write these as a matrix with one **row per input**: every row is a probability distribution, so it sums to 1.

steps.prompt: Rows are inputs and columns are outputs. Which matrix is a valid channel transition matrix?
steps.explanation: Each row lists the output probabilities for one input, so each row must be non-negative and sum to 1: 0.9 + 0.1 = 1 and 0.2 + 0.8 = 1. Two of the other matrices have columns, not rows, that sum to 1, and the remaining one contains a negative 'probability'.

steps.prompt: A BSC flips each bit with probability {{p}}. The transmitter sends a 1 with probability {{s}}. What is $P(Y = 1)$?
steps.explanation: A 1 arrives either as a sent 1 that was not flipped or as a sent 0 that was flipped: $P(Y=1)$ = {{s}} × {{1-p}} + {{1-s}} × {{p}} = **{{s*(1-p) + (1-s)*p||3}}**. Noise pulls the output towards 0.5.

steps.title: Capacity
steps.body: How much information gets through depends on the channel and on the input distribution. The **capacity** is the best you can do: the maximum of $I(X;Y)$ over all input distributions, in bits per channel use. A noiseless channel with $M$ input symbols carries $\log_2 M$ bits per use.

steps.prompt: A noiseless channel accepts one of {{M}} symbols per use and is used {{rs||7}} times per second.

ask.prompt: What is its capacity per channel use?
ask.explanation: Noiseless: every input is recognised, so use all {{M}} equally often: $C = \log_2 {{M}}$ = **{{log2(M)}} bits per use**.

ask.prompt: What is its capacity in bit/s?

steps.prompt: The capacity of a channel changes when the transmitter starts sending one input symbol more often than another.
steps.explanation: False. $I(X;Y)$ changes with the input distribution, but the capacity is the **maximum** over all input distributions, a property of the channel alone. A badly chosen input distribution simply transfers less than $C$.

steps.prompt: A BSC with $p$ = {{p}} is driven by a source that sends a 1 with probability {{s}}. Find $I(X;Y)$.

steps.title: The binary symmetric channel
steps.body: The BSC flips each bit with probability $p$. With a uniform input, $C = 1 - H(p)$. Drag $p$: capacity is 1 at both ends (at $p$ = 1 every bit is inverted, which the receiver can undo) and 0 at $p$ = 0.5, where the output is independent of the input.

steps.prompt: What is the capacity of a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability {{p}}?
Drag the crossover probability $p$ (at most 0.5) until the BSC has a capacity of {{c}} bit per use.
steps.explanation: $1 - H(p)$ = {{c}} needs $H(p)$ = {{1-c}}, which happens at $p$ ≈ **{{pt||2}}**. Note how fast capacity falls: a few percent of flipped bits already cost a large part of the channel.

steps.title: The binary erasure channel
steps.body: The BEC delivers each bit correctly with probability $1 - \varepsilon$ and otherwise outputs an erasure mark 'e': the receiver knows which bits are missing. Its capacity is $1 - \varepsilon$: exactly the fraction of bits that arrive.

steps.prompt: A packet link loses {{e}} % of its packets (lost packets are detected). Each packet carries {{b}} bits and {{r}} packets are sent per second. What is the capacity of the link?
steps.explanation: Detected losses are erasures: $C = (1 - \varepsilon)$ = {{1 - e/100}} of the raw rate. Raw rate = {{r}} × {{b}} = {{r*b|bit/s}}, so $C$ = **{{r*b*(1 - e/100)|bit/s}}**.

steps.prompt: One link flips bits with probability {{p}} (BSC), another erases them with probability {{p}} (BEC). Which has the higher capacity?
steps.explanation: BEC: $C = 1 - \varepsilon$ = **{{1-p}}**. BSC: $C = 1 - H({{p}})$ = **{{(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))}}**. An erasure says 'this bit is unknown'; a flip hides among the correct bits, so finding and fixing it costs much more redundancy.

steps.prompt: A binary symmetric channel with $p$ = 1 (every bit is inverted) has zero capacity.
steps.explanation: False. $C = 1 - H(1) = 1 - 0$ = **1 bit**: the receiver simply inverts every bit. A channel is useless only when its output is independent of its input, as for $p$ = 0.5.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows the capacity of a binary symmetric channel as a function of its crossover probability $p$?
steps.explanation: $C = 1 - H(p)$: 1 at $p$ = 0 and $p$ = 1, 0 at $p$ = 0.5, with rounded (not straight) sides. The hill is $H(p)$ itself, the straight line $1 - p$ is the erasure channel, and the V-shape $|1 - 2p|$ has the right end points but the wrong shape.

steps.title: Shannon's speed limit
steps.body: A code maps $k$ message bits to $n$ channel symbols, a rate of $R = k/n$ bits per use. For any $R < C$, long enough codes make the error probability as small as you like; for $R > C$ it stays bounded away from zero. In bit/s: capacity per use × channel uses per second.

steps.prompt: A BSC with $p$ = {{p}} is used at {{rs|baud}} (channel uses per second). What is the highest information rate that can be sent reliably?
steps.explanation: $C = 1 - H({{p}})$ = 1 − {{(-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12)))}} = {{(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))}} bit per use. × {{rs|baud}}: **{{rs*(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))|bit/s}}**. Any rate below that is possible with good enough coding.

steps.prompt: Codewords of $n$ = {{n}} bits are sent over a BSC with $p$ = {{p}}. What is the largest number of message bits $k$ for which the rate $k/n$ stays below capacity?
steps.explanation: $C = 1 - H({{p}})$ = {{(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))||4}}. Need $k < nC$ = {{n}} × {{(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))||4}} = {{n*(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))||4}}, so $k$ = **{{floor(n*(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12)))))}}**. (The theorem promises reliability only for long codes; short codes need a margin.)

steps.prompt: A ternary channel keeps each symbol with probability {{1-p}} and turns it into each of the two other symbols with probability {{p/2}}. What is its capacity?
steps.explanation: The channel is symmetric, so $C = \log_2 3 - H(\text{row})$ with row ({{1-p}}, {{p/2}}, {{p/2}}): $H$ = {{-(1-p)*log2(1-p) - p*log2(p/2)||3}} bits. $C$ = 1.585 − {{-(1-p)*log2(1-p) - p*log2(p/2)||3}} = **{{log2(3) + (1-p)*log2(1-p) + p*log2(p/2)||3}} bits per use**.

steps.prompt: A channel has {{M}} input symbols arranged in a circle. Each symbol arrives either unchanged or as the next symbol around the circle (clockwise), with probability 1/2 each. What is its capacity?
steps.explanation: The channel is symmetric with rows (1/2, 1/2, 0, …), so $C = \log_2 {{M}} - H(1/2, 1/2)$ = {{log2(M)}} − 1 = **{{log2(M) - 1}} bits per use**. Using only every other symbol achieves it with zero errors: the {{M/2}} used symbols can never be confused.

steps.prompt: Match each channel to its capacity.
steps.explanation: Noiseless: $\log_2 M$. BSC: $1 - H(p)$, which is 0 at $p$ = 0.5 and 0.5 at $p$ = 0.11 (since $H(0.11)$ = 0.5). BEC: $1 - \varepsilon$.

steps.prompt: Codes of rate {{R}} exist that reach an arbitrarily small error probability on a BSC with $p$ = {{p}}, provided their block length is large enough.
steps.explanation: $C = 1 - H({{p}})$ = {{(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))||3}} bit per use. The coding theorem allows exactly the rates **below** $C$, so compare: rate $R$ = {{R}} against $C$ = {{(1 - (-(p)*log2(max(p, 1e-12)) - (1-(p))*log2(max(1-(p), 1e-12))))||3}}. Above $C$, no code can make errors rare, however long.

steps.prompt: A {{F}}-Mbit file must cross a BSC with $p$ = {{p}} at {{rs|baud}}. What is the shortest possible transfer time with ideal coding?

steps.title: Channels in series
steps.body: When the output of one channel feeds the next without decoding in between, the chain is a single channel with a worse transition matrix. For BSCs the bit is wrong at the end if an **odd** number of hops flipped it. By the data-processing inequality the cascade can never have more capacity than its weakest link.

steps.prompt: Two BSCs with $p_1$ = {{p1}} and $p_2$ = {{p2}} are connected in series (no decoding in between).

ask.prompt: What is the crossover probability of the cascade?
ask.explanation: Wrong at the end only if exactly one hop flips: $p$ = {{p1}} × {{1-p2}} + {{p2}} × {{1-p1}} = **{{pe||4}}** (two flips cancel).

ask.prompt: What is the capacity of the cascade?

steps.prompt: A signal passes {{n}} identical regenerating hops, each a BSC with $p$ = {{p}} (bits are re-sent without error correction).

ask.prompt: What is the end-to-end crossover probability?

steps.prompt: A packet passes two links that lose (detectably) {{e1}} % and {{e2}} % of the packets. What is the capacity of the chain as a fraction of the raw rate?
steps.explanation: A packet survives only if both links deliver it: $1 - \varepsilon$ = {{1 - e1/100}} × {{1 - e2/100}} = **{{(1 - e1/100)*(1 - e2/100)||4}}**. For erasure channels the capacities simply multiply.

steps.prompt: Channels with capacities $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected in series, without decoding in between. What can you say about the capacity $C$ of the cascade?
options: $C = C_1 C_2$ for any two channels
steps.explanation: $X \to Y \to Z$ is a Markov chain, so $I(X;Z) \le I(X;Y) \le C_1$, and also $I(X;Z) \le C_2$ because $Z$ only sees what the second channel delivers. $C = C_1C_2$ happens to hold for erasure channels, but not for BSCs.

steps.prompt: BPSK over a noisy radio link with hard decisions acts as a BSC with $p = Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})$. The link has $E_b/N_0$ = {{x}} dB.

ask.prompt: What is the capacity of the resulting BSC?
ask.explanation: $p = Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})$ = {{pb||3}}, so $C = 1 - H({{pb||3}})$ = **{{(1 - (-(pb)*log2(max(pb, 1e-12)) - (1-(pb))*log2(max(1-(pb), 1e-12))))||3}} bit per use**. Hard decisions throw away reliability information; the next unit shows that the Gaussian channel itself carries more.

steps.prompt: A chain of identical hops, each a BSC with $p$ = {{p}}, is extended hop by hop. Drag $n$ to the **smallest** number of hops at which the end-to-end capacity has dropped below 0.5 bit.
